steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on synthesizing recursion-free programs from first-order functional specifications using saturation-based theorem proving (implemented in Vampire). Explain the setting, give our approach in a nutshell, and list the contributions with section pointers.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Program synthesis is about constructing code from a given specification. In this work we focus on synthesis from functional specifications that are summarized by valid first-order formulas, so our programs are provably correct. Synthesis is a powerful alternative to formal verification, but it faces intrinsic computational challenges. One of these challenges is for the reasoning backend that handles the program specifications, because the specifications typically include first-order quantifier alternations and interpreted theory symbols. So efficient reasoning with both theories and quantifiers is imperative for any program synthesis effort.

In this paper we address this demand for recursion-free programs. We use first-order theorem proving to extract code from correctness proofs of functional specifications, given as first-order formulas \forall\overline{x}.\exists y.F[\overline{x},y]. These formulas say that “for all (program) inputs \overline{x} there exists an output y such that the input-output relation (program computation) F[\overline{x},y] is valid”. Given such a specification, we synthesize a recursion-free program and we also derive a proof that certifies that the program satisfies the specification.

The programs we synthesize are built from first-order theory terms extended with \mathtt{if}\!-\!\mathtt{then}\!-\!\mathtt{else} constructors. We want our programs to yield computational models, i.e., they should be evaluable for given values of the input variables \overline{x}, so we restrict the synthesized programs to contain only computable symbols.

## Our approach in a nutshell.
- approach: saturation-based proving + answer literals track substitutions into y = program fragments
  - branch \mathtt{if}\ C\ \mathtt{then}\ r with C, r computable -> store, continue assuming \lnot C (branch conditions)
  - stop when conjunction of negated branch conditions unsatisfiable; assemble branches (Examples 1 - 3)
- challenges: (i) if-then-else construction inside proof search; (ii) only computable branch conditions and programs
## Contributions.
- semantics for answer-literal clauses + saturation algorithm, correct and computable programs (Section 4)
- calculus properties, extended superposition, computable unifiers (Section 5)
- unification for computable unifiers (Section 6)
- Vampire implementation and evaluation (Section 7); specs not expressible in SyGuS

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Program synthesis is about constructing code from a given specification. In this work we focus on synthesis from functional specifications that are summarized by valid first-order formulas, so our programs are provably correct. Synthesis is a powerful alternative to formal verification, but it faces intrinsic computational challenges. One of these challenges is for the reasoning backend that handles the program specifications, because the specifications typically include first-order quantifier alternations and interpreted theory symbols. So efficient reasoning with both theories and quantifiers is imperative for any program synthesis effort.

In this paper we address this demand for recursion-free programs. We use first-order theorem proving to extract code from correctness proofs of functional specifications, given as first-order formulas \forall\overline{x}.\exists y.F[\overline{x},y]. These formulas say that “for all (program) inputs \overline{x} there exists an output y such that the input-output relation (program computation) F[\overline{x},y] is valid”. Given such a specification, we synthesize a recursion-free program and we also derive a proof that certifies that the program satisfies the specification.

The programs we synthesize are built from first-order theory terms extended with \mathtt{if}\!-\!\mathtt{then}\!-\!\mathtt{else} constructors. We want our programs to yield computational models, i.e., they should be evaluable for given values of the input variables \overline{x}, so we restrict the synthesized programs to contain only computable symbols.

## Our approach in a nutshell.

To synthesize a recursion-free program, we prove its functional specification with saturation-based theorem proving. We extend the saturation-based proof search with answer literals, which lets us track substitutions into the output variable y of the specification. These substitutions correspond to the program fragments we are looking for, and they are conditioned on the clauses they are associated with in the proof. When we derive a clause that corresponds to a program branch \mathtt{if}\ C\ \mathtt{then}\ r, where C is a condition and r a term and both C,r are computable, we store it and we continue the proof search assuming that \lnot C holds. We call such conditions C (program) branch conditions. The saturation process, both for proof search and for code construction, terminates when the conjunction of the negations of the collected branch conditions becomes unsatisfiable. Then we assemble the recorded program branches into the final program, which satisfies the given (and proved) specification (see e.g. Examples 1 - 3).

There are two main challenges in making our approach effective: (i) integrating the construction of programs with \mathtt{if}\!-\!\mathtt{then}\!-\!\mathtt{else} into the proof search, so that proof search becomes program search/synthesis, and (ii) guiding program synthesis to only computable branch conditions and programs.

## Contributions.

Our contributions that solve the above challenges are the following:

- We formalize the semantics for clauses with answer literals and we introduce a saturation-based algorithm for program synthesis based on this semantics. We prove that if the inference system is sound, our saturation algorithm derives correct and computable programs (Section 4).

- We define properties that a sound inference calculus needs so that it is suitable for our saturation-based program synthesis algorithm. We extend the superposition calculus accordingly and we define a class of substitutions to use in the extended calculus, which we call computable unifiers (Section 5).

- We extend a first-order unification algorithm so that it finds computable unifiers (Section 6), which are then used in saturation-based program synthesis.

- We implement our work in the Vampire prover and evaluate the synthesis approach on a number of examples, where it complements other techniques in the area (Section 7). For example, the results show that our work can synthesize programs for specifications that cannot even be encoded in the SyGuS syntax.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Program synthesis constructs code from a given specification. In this work we focus on synthesis using functional specifications summarized by valid first-order formulas [1,2], ensuring that our programs are provably correct. While synthesis is a powerful alternative to formal verification [3], it faces intrinsic computational challenges. One of these challenges is posed to the reasoning backend used for handling program specifications, as these typically include first-order quantifier alternations and interpreted theory symbols. Efficient reasoning with both theories and quantifiers is therefore imperative for any effort towards program synthesis.

In this paper we address this demand for recursion-free programs. We advocate the use of first-order theorem proving for extracting code from correctness proofs of functional specifications given as first-order formulas \forall\overline{x}.\exists y.F[\overline{x},y]. These formulas state that “for all (program) inputs \overline{x} there exists an output y such that the input-output relation (program computation) F[\overline{x},y] is valid”. Given such a specification, we synthesize a recursion-free program and at the same time derive a proof certifying that the program satisfies the specification.

The programs we synthesize are built using first-order theory terms extended with \mathtt{if}\!-\!\mathtt{then}\!-\!\mathtt{else} constructors. To ensure that our programs yield computational models, i.e., that they can be evaluated for given values of input variables \overline{x}, we restrict the synthesized programs to contain only computable symbols.

## Our approach in a nutshell.

In order to synthesize a recursion-free program, we prove its functional specification using saturation-based theorem proving [4,5]. We extend saturation-based proof search with answer literals [6], which allows us to track substitutions into the output variable y of the specification. These substitutions correspond to the sought program fragments and are conditioned on the clauses they are associated with in the proof. When we derive a clause corresponding to a program branch \mathtt{if}\ C\ \mathtt{then}\ r, where C is a condition and r a term and both C,r are computable, we store it and continue proof search assuming that \lnot C holds; we refer to such conditions C as (program) branch conditions. The saturation process for both proof search and code construction terminates when the conjunction of negations of the collected branch conditions becomes unsatisfiable. We then synthesize the final program satisfying the given (and proved) specification by assembling the recorded program branches (see e.g. Examples 1 - 3).

The main challenges in making our approach effective are (i) integrating the construction of programs with \mathtt{if}\!-\!\mathtt{then}\!-\!\mathtt{else} into the proof search, thus turning proof search into program search/synthesis, and (ii) guiding program synthesis to only computable branch conditions and programs.

## Contributions.

We make the following contributions to solve the above challenges:

- We formalize the semantics for clauses with answer literals and introduce a saturation-based algorithm for program synthesis based on this semantics. We prove that, given a sound inference system, our saturation algorithm derives correct and computable programs (Section 4).

- We define properties of a sound inference calculus that make the calculus suitable for our saturation-based program synthesis algorithm. Accordingly, we extend the superposition calculus and define a class of substitutions to be used within the extended calculus, which we call computable unifiers (Section 5).

- We extend a first-order unification algorithm to find computable unifiers (Section 6), to be further used in saturation-based program synthesis.

- We implement our work in the Vampire prover [5] and evaluate our synthesis approach on a number of examples, complementing other techniques in the area (Section 7). For example, our results demonstrate that our work applies to synthesizing programs for specifications that cannot even be encoded in the SyGuS syntax [7].
